Netherlands: after two days behind closed doors at an estate near Hilversum, the Jetten government is still standing, but the liberal right speaks of a “failed experiment”

On Saturday, November 14, and Sunday, November 15, the leaders of the three Dutch government parties, D66, VVD and CDA, continued their crisis talks at the De Zwaluwenberg estate near Hilversum, after the quarrel over a “millionaires' tax.” The coalition has not collapsed, but no agreement has been announced [1][2][3][4].

The crisis was born of a vote: the amended version of the tax plan was passed by a single vote in the lower house, thanks to a compromise between D66, the CDA and two opposition parties, PRO and Volt [6].
This compromise creates a higher tax bracket for income above 60,000 euros from savings and assets. PRO leader Jesse Klaver called it a “millionaires' tax,” and the VVD voted against it [6].
On Friday, more than seven hours of meetings had settled nothing; Prime Minister Rob Jetten had gotten the parties to keep talking [1][5].
Over the weekend, the negotiations moved to the De Zwaluwenberg estate; according to NOS, VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz made it known that her party did not want to continue on this basis [3].
After two days, the coalition had still not emerged from the crisis, and talks were to continue at the Catshuis, the Prime Minister's residence in The Hague, according to radio station BNR [4].

A group of former senior officials and constitutional experts has urged the parties not to bring down the minority government; a “restart” proposal from Christian Union leader Bikker has already won a majority [2].

Key takeaway: Rob Jetten's government is a minority government and must find votes in the opposition for every bill. By teaming up with the left on taxes, D66 and the CDA angered their third partner, the VVD, which accuses them of betraying the coalition agreement [1][5].
Dilan Yeşilgöz calls this government a “failed experiment,” but the VVD is staying for now. Its parliamentary leader, Ruben Brekelmans, is demanding a “fundamental reset” of the coalition [1][5].

If it fell, forming a new majority would be very difficult, and early elections would come barely nine months after the government took office [2][7]. MPs have already passed a motion calling for other alliances to be explored before returning to the polls [8].

The substance of the debate affects all of Europe: how to tax wealth more to fund budgets under pressure, without driving savings away. The Netherlands is looking for an answer in the middle of a political crisis, with a tax plan for next year that still has to find a majority [6][8].

France is also debating taxes on the largest fortunes, with a 2027 budget that has no majority. The Dutch crisis shows the same trap: a tax measure popular with part of the opposition can blow up a fragile coalition.

South China Sea: Australia and the Philippines sign a new defense agreement in Manila, replacing the 1995 one

On Sunday, November 15, on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Manila and in the presence of Anthony Albanese, Australia and the Philippines signed a defense cooperation agreement that replaces a thirty-year-old text: maritime surveillance, intelligence sharing, exercises and military infrastructure, in the face of Chinese pressure [1][2][3].

The text was signed by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Australian Ambassador Marc Innes-Brown, before Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who was in town for the ASEAN summit [2][3].
It replaces the 1995 memorandum of understanding on defense cooperation, which had become too narrow for military relations that have grown considerably [1][2].

According to the Australian government, it covers maritime awareness and activities, information sharing, strategic dialogue, training, interoperability (the ability of the two militaries to act together) and defense infrastructure [1].

Gilberto Teodoro told the Manila Times that the agreement provides a single framework for implementing the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, in force since 2012, which allows Australian troops to train on Philippine soil [3].
According to AFP, cited by Arab News, the goal is to strengthen deterrence in the region, as incidents with the Chinese coast guard multiply in the South China Sea [4][5].

On August 7 in Darwin, the two countries' defense ministers, Richard Marles and Gilberto Teodoro, had already condemned Chinese actions against Philippine vessels and pledged to conclude this text [7][8].

In Manila, Anthony Albanese also said he welcomed the prospect of a meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, and did not rule out appearing in the APEC group photo next to the Russian president [6][10].

Key takeaway: Australia is stepping up its commitment to the Philippines, on the front line facing China in the South China Sea. This is not an alliance with a mutual defense obligation, but a framework for training, monitoring the sea and building military facilities together [1][3].

Chinese pressure has increased sharply around Scarborough Shoal, claimed by both countries: the number of days the Chinese coast guard was present there rose from 516 in 2024 to 1,099 in 2025, and in April 2026 Beijing installed a 352-meter floating barrier at the entrance to the lagoon, according to an analysis by the University of Technology Sydney [9].
For Manila, having multiple partners (United States, Japan, Australia, Canada) means not depending on a single ally in the face of Beijing.
The timing is delicate: China remains Australia's largest customer, and Anthony Albanese is due to travel to Shenzhen for APEC, where Xi Jinping will host Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin [6][10].

A large share of the Asian electronics and goods arriving in Europe passes through the South China Sea. Every agreement that strengthens deterrence aims to avoid a conflict that would block these routes and send shipping costs soaring, as we are seeing today with Hormuz.

Lebanon: Trump's UN envoy, Mike Waltz, in Beirut to prepare for the post-UNIFIL era, with a monitoring mission modeled on the Sinai

Arriving in Beirut on Sunday, November 15, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz is discussing what will replace UNIFIL, the UN peacekeeping force in South Lebanon whose mandate ends on December 31. Washington is considering a mission inspired by the one that monitors the peace between Egypt and Israel [1][2][3].

Mike Waltz is due to meet President Joseph Aoun on Monday morning, then Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri; the US embassy has announced a tour of Lebanon and Morocco from November 15 to 17 [1][4][5].

According to The New Arab, citing Lebanese media and Asharq Bloomberg, the Trump administration is studying a mechanism modeled on the Multinational Force and Observers (MFO), which has monitored the Sinai since the Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty [3][6].

Two arrangements are under discussion: one to verify Hezbollah's disarmament and prevent it from re-establishing itself militarily in the south, the other to facilitate humanitarian aid to border villages [1].
UNIFIL's mandate ends on December 31, 2026; the withdrawal is to begin that day and last up to a year [1].

On the Lebanese side, sources say they have not been informed of the content of the proposals and reject any arrangement not placed under the aegis of the UN, the European Union or influential countries; Beirut is interested in a European force proposed by France and Italy if UNIFIL cannot stay [1][7].
On the ground, the Israeli army said on Saturday it had destroyed a 35-meter Hezbollah tunnel in Majdal Zoun, and says it remains committed to the ceasefire [8].

Key takeaway: UNIFIL, the UN peacekeeping force in South Lebanon, is going to leave, and no one yet knows who will take its place. Washington wants an arrangement focused on Hezbollah's disarmament, while Beirut wants to keep an international framework [1][3].

The deadlock is well known: Israel refuses to leave the positions it occupies in Lebanon as long as Hezbollah keeps its weapons, and Hezbollah, backed by Iran, refuses to give them up as long as the Israeli army remains on Lebanese soil [1].

The choice of model matters. The Sinai MFO is not a UN mission: transposing it to Lebanon would give Washington a central role in monitoring the border. The mandate, powers, composition and coordination with the Lebanese army of such a force remain unclear [3][6].

France is directly concerned: French soldiers serve in UNIFIL, and Paris and Rome are pushing a European option [7]. The United States is in talks with these two countries, according to The New Arab [3].

France has soldiers in South Lebanon with UNIFIL: the shape of the post-UNIFIL arrangement will decide whether they stay, leave or change mission. A stable Lebanon also means less risk of a new front in a region already shaken by the war with Iran, which weighs on the price of your energy.

Brazil: “Instead of crying, we looked for other partners,” Lula says in Manila, where he wants to double trade with Southeast Asia

On Sunday, November 15, at the ASEAN summit in Manila, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva explained that Brazil had responded to Donald Trump's tariffs by diversifying its customers: the United States now accounts for only 9.2% of Brazil's foreign trade, according to him. He wants to double trade with ASEAN [1][2][5].

As a guest of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Lula made the first visit by a sitting Brazilian president to the Philippines on November 14 and 15, before attending the ASEAN summit as a guest of the chair [4].
“Instead of crying, we looked for other partners,” he said, referring to US tariffs, adding that his government had refused to go begging to Washington [1][2].

According to the figures he presented, the United States now accounts for only 9.2% of Brazil's foreign trade, while trade has grown by about 20% with China, 15.8% with Germany, 15% with Indonesia and 13% with Vietnam [5][2].
Trade between Brazil and the ten ASEAN countries reached $38.4 billion in 2025, compared with $3 billion in 2003, according to Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira; Lula wants to double it [5][3].
Brasília hopes to become a full ASEAN “dialogue partner” in 2027, Mauro Vieira said [5].

Brazil and the Philippines signed two memoranda of understanding, one to facilitate agricultural trade, the other against anticompetitive practices, as Manila, the largest buyer of Brazilian pork, has just suspended its imports for two months [3][2].
Lula also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to move toward concluding a free trade agreement between Mercosur and Canada [5].

Key takeaway: Brazil illustrates a global trend. Faced with US protectionism, major exporters are turning to Asia, Europe and Canada. Southeast Asia is a sought-after outlet for Brazilian soybeans, meat and ore [1][3].

The 9.2% figure is the one put forward by Lula, and should be read as a political message: his government had to create an aid plan, “Brasil Soberano,” for sectors hit by US tariffs, and this plan still needs new phases, notes the Gazeta do Povo [2].

The trip comes at a pivotal moment: re-elected in October for a fourth term that begins on January 1, Lula is due back in Brazil on Monday evening and to start forming his new government this week, according to Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, who is acting president in the interim [6][7].

The name of Fernando Haddad, defeated in the race for governor of São Paulo, is circulating for a return to his former ministry, and Lula will have to negotiate with several centrist parties to keep a majority in Congress, where Jair Bolsonaro's Liberal Party has grown stronger [7].

Brazil is also negotiating with Europe under the EU-Mercosur agreement, which French farmers oppose. The more customers it finds elsewhere, in Asia or Canada, the stronger its position against Brussels. For you, what is at stake is where some of the beef, chicken, coffee and orange juice you buy comes from.

news.2026-11-16-chili-kast-popularite-18: Chile: eight months after taking office, José Antonio Kast falls to 18% approval, dragged down by a sentence-reduction scandal and 9.8% unemployment

On Sunday, November 15, the Criteria poll put Chilean President José Antonio Kast's popularity at 18%, six points lower in one week, with 72% unfavorable opinions. 79% of respondents oppose him keeping his Justice Minister, Fernando Rabat, who is the target of impeachment proceedings [1][2][3].
According to the Agenda Criteria survey, 18% of Chileans approve of the president's performance, compared with 24% a week earlier; 72% disapprove, compared with 67% [1][3][4].
These are exactly the figures recorded by Sebastián Piñera in December 2021, at the end of his term, El Mostrador points out [2].

At the heart of the drop: Justice Minister Fernando Rabat, after the government admitted an error in granting sentence reductions. 79% of respondents oppose him staying in office, 16% support him and 5% have no opinion [1][2].

The opposition is preparing a “constitutional accusation” against him, Chile's impeachment procedure, in three chapters: sentence reductions granted to people convicted of sexual violence against minors and of crimes against humanity, benefits for 115 foreigners convicted of drug trafficking, and information given to Congress [2][11].
Among respondents who know about this procedure, 68% approve of filing it; but its launch was delayed again last week, for lack of agreement on the left about its legal grounds [2][6][7].
Other pollsters confirm the trend: the Black & White institute measured only 20% favorable opinions in early November [9].

In the background, unemployment rose to 9.8% in the third quarter according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), 1.3 points higher than a year earlier: more than one million people (1,007,976) are looking for work [5].

Key takeaway: elected on the promise of restoring order and reviving the economy, José Antonio Kast, who took office in March, is seeing his popularity collapse on both fronts at once: justice, with the sentence-reduction scandal, and jobs, with unemployment at a high [1][5].
Unemployment affects women (10.5%) more than men (9.3%), and reaches 10.4% in the Santiago region. The number of people employed fell 1.1% in one year, while more people are looking for work [5].

Pressure is also mounting within his own camp: before his return from a European tour, the right-wing coalition Chile Vamos called for better government coordination, amid rumors of a cabinet reshuffle [10].

What is at stake in the proceedings against Fernando Rabat is arithmetic: the opposition does not have a majority on its own in the Chamber of Deputies and needs votes from the right, which explains its hesitation [6][7].

Chile is the world's largest copper producer, a key metal for electric cars, power grids and the electronics you buy. A weakened government, with rising unemployment, may have a harder time passing its mining and tax reforms, something European manufacturers who depend on this copper are watching.

Cape Verde: José Maria Neves re-elected in the first round with nearly 64% of the vote, but two out of three voters stayed home

On Sunday, November 15, Cape Verde's President José Maria Neves was re-elected in the first round with about 63.8% of the vote, far ahead of former Justice Minister Joana Rosa, who conceded defeat. Abstention reached about 68%, compared with 52% in 2021 [1][2][3].

With 96.8% of polling stations counted, José Maria Neves, backed by the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), had 80,018 votes, or 63.8%, a lead of 40,358 votes over his main rival [2][11].

Joana Rosa, a former Justice Minister backed by the Movement for Democracy (MpD) and the first woman to run for president of the archipelago, won about 31.6% and conceded defeat in the evening [3][11].
More than 50% of the votes cast were needed to win in the first round; otherwise a runoff would have been held [2].
Abstention reached about 68%, compared with 52% in the 2021 presidential election, according to provisional results [4][2].

Joana Rosa called this abstention a “black spot on our democracy”; José Maria Neves, who spoke of “an excellent victory,” said he had sensed this “high abstention” during his visits to the islands and to the diaspora [3][5].
Six candidates were running. A former Prime Minister, José Maria Neves had announced on September 14 that he would seek a second five-year term [10].
The results remain provisional until they are officially proclaimed by the National Elections Commission [1][2].

Key takeaway: Cape Verde, an Atlantic archipelago often cited as one of Africa's most stable democracies, confirms the shift to the left that began in the spring. On May 17, the PAICV won the legislative elections with an absolute majority, 37 seats out of 72, ending ten years of MpD government [6][7].

The president and the government are now from the same camp: Prime Minister Francisco Carvalho, who also holds the Finance portfolio, was appointed by José Maria Neves in June [6][7]. This should make it easier to pass reforms, but the record abstention shows strong voter fatigue.

The economy depends mainly on tourism: it grew 6.3% in 2025, and the World Bank forecasts 4.8% in 2026, held back by the conflict in the Middle East. Public debt fell to 100.7% of GDP in 2025, but servicing it still absorbs 34.2% of state revenue [8].
An IMF mission, from October 28 to November 6, praised fiscal management while warning of risks in the 2027 budget. The IMF's programs with Cape Verde are due to end in December [9].

Cape Verde is an increasingly popular holiday destination for the French and other Europeans, and a Portuguese-speaking country closely tied to Portugal, hence a large diaspora in Europe. A stable country, where power alternates through the ballot box, reassures tourism investors and the European Union, with which it cooperates on fishing and migration.

On Monday, November 16, Asian makers of chip equipment and memory slumped on the eve of Nvidia's earnings, expected Tuesday evening. In Tokyo, Advantest lost about 10% and Lasertec nearly 9%; in Seoul, the Kospi fell nearly 3% on selling by foreign investors [1][2][4][5].

In Tokyo, Advantest, which makes the machines used to test Nvidia's chips, fell about 10% during the session, and Lasertec, a specialist in photomask inspection, fell 8.8% to more than 9% depending on the readings; Tokyo Electron fell 5.2% [2][3].

Foreign investors sold about 852 billion won of Korean shares, worried about the strength of the artificial intelligence boom [4][5][6].
Two pieces of bad economic news also weighed: Japan's GDP shrank in the third quarter, a first in a year, and China's October figures disappointed [1][7].
Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 17, after Wall Street closes; its stock lost 13% last week, its worst week since April 2025 [7][8].
Key takeaway: in Asia, dozens of companies live off Nvidia's orders. When doubts grow about its next numbers, investors sell its suppliers first, even before knowing the result [1][2].

The doubt stems from the abrupt departure of Jensen Huang, CEO for 33 years, on November 12: Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will present the results on an interim basis. Markets are wondering whether the AI investment strategy will stay the same [1][9].

How it works: why suppliers fall even before the results

A stock is worth what investors think the company will earn tomorrow. Advantest or Tokyo Electron sell their machines to chipmakers, which in turn produce for Nvidia: if Nvidia slows its orders, the whole chain suffers, with an amplified effect at the end of the chain. On the eve of an uncertain event, many fund managers prefer to reduce their exposure rather than place a bet: they sell, even if it means buying back later [1]. Because the Tokyo and Seoul indexes are heavily concentrated in these stocks, a few shares are enough to drag the whole market down: on Monday, two companies accounted for 904 of the 960 points lost by the Nikkei [2][3]. If Nvidia's numbers reassure, the move can reverse just as quickly, as on November 9 [13].

Iron ore: China slows more than expected, the price clings to $90 a ton and Australia's mining giants slip

On Monday, November 16, Beijing released weaker-than-expected October figures: industrial output up 4.8%, retail sales up 0.4%, property investment down 21.6%. Iron ore, which just had its worst week in five weeks, is holding around $90 a ton, and BHP is down 2% in Sydney [1][3][4].
In October, Chinese industrial output grew 4.8% year on year, compared with 5.3% expected and 5.5% in September; retail sales rose only 0.4%, compared with 0.8% expected [3][4].
Over the first ten months of the year, investment in equipment and buildings fell 8.1%, more than at the end of September (−7.2%); property investment plunged 21.6% and home sales 14.1% [3].

Yet real estate and construction are the biggest consumers of steel, and therefore of iron ore. The December contract in Singapore, the global benchmark, stayed around $90.40 a ton, after a 2.8% drop last week, its worst week in five weeks [1][2].
In China's ten major ports, ore inventories swelled by 3.3 million tons in one week, to 108 million tons, according to Shanghai Metals Market, a sign that steel mills are buying less [6].
On the Sydney stock exchange, the ASX 200 index fell for the third session in a row, weighed down by mining stocks; BHP, the world's largest miner, was down 2% in the afternoon [1][5].
Copper also fell to its lowest level in nearly four months [2].
BHP held an investor briefing on Monday, just as the price of its main product is stagnating [1][2].

Key takeaway: iron ore is the thermometer of Chinese construction. China is by far the world's largest buyer of ore, and its October figures show a property sector still in crisis: as long as fewer homes are built, steel demand will not pick up [3][4].

The $90-a-ton threshold matters: analysts see it both as a technical limit for markets and as the level below which the most expensive mines become barely profitable [1][2]. At the end of October, ore had already ended the month at its lowest level since October 2022 [7].

Beijing also weighs on prices in another way: CMRG, a state buyer, centralizes Chinese purchases to negotiate with miners. In July, it had asked steel mills to stop taking certain Fortescue ores after July 15, and the Australian group had denounced a threat to the stability of deliveries [8][9].

Australian miners are caught in a vise: on one side a falling price, on the other a single Chinese buyer that negotiates hard. BHP has signed an agreement with CMRG, but Fortescue is still waiting for its own, and its targets for fiscal year 2027 remain contingent on that agreement [10][11].

Cheap iron ore eventually makes steel a little cheaper, for cars, household appliances or construction in Europe. But a Chinese slowdown also means fewer orders for European exporters, from autos to luxury goods, and it is often bad news for jobs.

How it works: from Chinese construction sites to BHP's share price

Iron ore is used to make steel, and China is by far the world's largest producer. When Beijing builds fewer towers and roads, its steel mills run less and buy less ore: inventories pile up in ports [6], and buyers negotiate prices down. The price is set mainly through futures contracts, in Singapore in dollars and in Dalian in yuan. For a miner like BHP or Fortescue, every dollar lost per ton is multiplied across hundreds of millions of tons sold each year: its profit, and therefore its share price, follow the price of ore. Investors therefore sell mining stocks as soon as Chinese figures disappoint, even before prices really fall [1][3].
